title: Nouns: gender and number

objectives.can: Give the gender and number of a noun, including the dual.
Recognise ten of the commonest nouns of the Hebrew Bible.

explanation.summary: A Hebrew noun is masculine or feminine, and singular, plural or (for some words) dual. The ending often tells you which, but not always, so you learn the pattern and the exceptions together.

sections.heading: Two genders
body: Every Hebrew noun has a grammatical gender: masculine or feminine. There is no neuter. The gender of a word like אֶרֶץ or עִיר has nothing to do with sex; it is a property of the word, and it shows in the adjectives and verbs that agree with it.

A feminine singular noun very often ends in -ָה or -ֶת, but many feminine nouns have no such ending. עִיר, 'city', is feminine; so are many words for paired parts of the body. Some words are used in both genders, and the analysed text marks these as common gender. This lesson asks about nouns that the texts mark clearly as masculine or feminine.

sections.heading: The plural
body: The ordinary masculine plural ends in -ִים and the ordinary feminine plural in -וֹת. So יוֹם, 'day', has the plural יָמִים, and the feminine noun שָׁנֶה, 'year', has the plural שְׁנוֹת where it stands before another noun.

But the plural ending does not reliably show the gender. שָׁנֶה is feminine and yet has the plural שָׁנִים. אָב, 'father', is masculine and yet has the plural אָבוֹת. מָאוֹר, 'luminary', is masculine and has the plural מְאֹרֹת. Learn each noun's plural as part of the noun, and read the gender from the agreeing words, or from the dictionary.

The stem of the noun can also change when a plural ending is added: the vowels shift, as in the pair בֵּן and בָּנִים. A few nouns use a different stem altogether, such as אִישׁ, 'man', whose plural is אֲנָשִׁים.

sections.heading: The dual
body: Hebrew has a third number, the dual, ending in -ַיִם. It is used mostly for things that come naturally in pairs: יָדַיִם, 'two hands', and עֵינַיִם, 'two eyes'. It is also used for some measures of two, such as units of time or quantity. The dual is a small category, but the words in it are common.

Two very common words look like duals but are usually counted as plurals in form only: שָׁמַיִם, 'heavens', and מַיִם, 'water'. They have no singular, and the analysed text is not consistent about שָׁמַיִם: it records it as plural in some verses and as dual in others. Do not worry about this; recognise the ending and the word.

sections.heading: Which forms this lesson uses
body: Nouns appear in several shapes. They can carry the article, a prefixed preposition or a pronoun suffix, and they have a shorter form when joined to a following noun (the construct state). All of that comes in later lessons. Here you read the plain forms: absolute state, no suffix, no prefixed preposition or conjunction. The questions use real words of the Hebrew Bible and show each in its verse.

misunderstandings: A word ending in -ִים is not always masculine and a word ending in -וֹת is not always feminine. Look at the singular and at the words that agree with the noun.
A feminine noun does not always end in -ָה. עִיר is feminine with no ending at all.
The dual does not mean 'any two'. It is used for natural pairs and some fixed expressions; two of most things are written with the plural and the number 'two'.
Gender has nothing to do with the thing a noun names. A grammatical gender is a property of the word.

deeper.heading: Common gender and the word 'both genders'
body: Some nouns, such as אֶרֶץ, 'earth, land', are used in both genders in the Hebrew Bible, and the analysed text labels them common. Grammarians discuss these words at length. For a beginner the practical rule is simple: look at the verb or adjective that goes with the noun in the verse you are reading.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three plurals. מְאֹרֹת ends in -וֹת but the noun, 'luminary', is masculine. וּלְיָמִים is the masculine plural of 'day', with a conjunction and a preposition in front. וְשָׁנִים is the plural of 'year', a feminine noun, with the masculine-looking ending -ִים. The ending of the plural does not settle the gender.

quoted.title: Jeremiah
quoted.english: In those days they shall say no more: 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אָבוֹת is the plural of אָב, 'father': a masculine noun with the ending -וֹת. בָּנִים is the plural of בֵּן, 'son', with the usual masculine ending and a changed vowel in the stem. The two plurals stand in one saying about fathers and sons.

examples.analysis: עִיר, 'city', is feminine but has no feminine ending. שֵׁם, 'name', is masculine singular. The singular of both is the bare stem.

examples.analysis: The dual of יָד, 'hand': the ending -ַיִם in וְהַיָּדַיִם and the shorter form יְדֵי that is used before a following noun. Both are marked dual. The speaker is Isaac, who is feeling the hands of his son.
